#311. X implements parental controls for teen users

Elon Musk's social network X just got a new feature it never had under previous ownership.

That would be parental controls for teen users, to be exact. In a new post from the official Safety account on X, the company announced it has implemented parental controls for users aged 13 to 17. The way it works is that an account run by a parent or guardian establishes a supervisory link to the account run by a teen, which gives the parent or guardian access to a bunch of monitoring and safety features the site didn't have before.

These features include the ability to monitor usage and set daily limits for the teen, as well as the option to require new followers to be approved by the parent or guardian. Recommendations on the For You feed can be limited to accounts the teen already follows, while parents can mute specific words, control who can send direct messages, and see who the teens have chatted with in DMs without seeing the messages themselves.

As X noted, this only starts when both parties in the equation consent to it, so a teen cannot have their account limited against their will. Theoretically, anyway. A parent account can supervise as many as five teen accounts, but a teen account can only be linked to one parent account.

This is interesting because it's an acknowledgment by X that some teenagers do use the platform, but even in the Safety account's post, the company is clear that X is "not designed for or promoted to children." Indeed, one could argue that teen users should stay far away from a service that has become home to hate speech, widespread misinformation, and a Grok AI chatbot that has gotten up to plenty of unsavory business since it was introduced.

But if teens are going to use X, at least these features exist now.

#310. Some U.S. food banks see demand top pandemic levels

During the Covid-19 pandemic, Greg Silverman watched an MTA bus driver pull over on Manhattan's Upper West Side, let his passengers off and run across the street toward him.

Silverman, who runs New York nonprofit West Side Campaign Against Hunger, initially thought the driver wanted to use the bathroom at the church where the food distribution was taking place. Instead, the man asked, "Can I get some food?"

"He was a full-time employee," Silverman said. "You are an essential personnel, making the city survive and you need food."

Now, Silverman said, his organization has seen demand surpass even the levels it observed during that time of crisis when the U.S. economy ground to a halt — and many of the people now seeking food also have jobs. Silverman expects the nonprofit to distribute as much as 6 million pounds of food this year.

"The height of the pandemic was not the height of need, by any means," he said.

The pressure on the emergency food system extends beyond New York. Nationally, use of charitable food programs remains elevated as sustained inflation makes it harder for Americans to afford food, housing and healthcare. Higher prices come at the same time that the federal government has restricted food aid.

The Department of Agriculture's latest annual report found that 13.7% of U.S. households, roughly 18.3 million households, experienced food insecurity in 2024. That rate was significantly higher than in every year from 2016 through 2021.

The pandemic initially brought a surge in demand for charitable food programs, which was followed by government support. In the years that followed, pandemic-era policies such as expanded Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, benefits, the enhanced child tax credit and school meal programs phased out as inflation spiked.

"This is not because you can't go to work," said City Harvest President Carlos Rodriguez. "Primarily, your work and your wages are just not keeping up with the way costs have gone up in the last five years alone."

City Harvest, which works with food providers across the five boroughs of New York, told CNBC 1 in 5 New Yorkers is currently experiencing food insecurity, or limited access to enough food because of a lack of money or other resources. That is up from 1 in 6 a year earlier, and 1 in 8 before the pandemic.

Average monthly visits to food pantries and soup kitchens in New York are also 85% higher than before the pandemic, said Rodriguez.

In the Federal Reserve's October Beige Book, the central bank's New York regional branch described a sharp rise in first-time food pantry users. One nonprofit leader told the Federal Reserve Bank of New York that the strain was comparable to the pandemic, "but without the same philanthropic and government support."

Data from Plentiful, a technology platform that connects people with food pantries and tracks their usage, also points to growing demand and limited resources.

"For pantries using our reservation and pre-registration features, we see that the overwhelming majority of those are at or over capacity," said Catherine Compitello, CEO of Plentiful. "Demand is growing while supply is not."

First-time users of Plentiful in New York City rose roughly 56% from August to October, Compitello said. It was the second-largest fall surge since 2016; the only larger one came during last year's federal government shutdown, when delayed SNAP benefits drove more people to seek food assistance.

Compitello said that when families have trouble affording essentials, they often prioritize healthcare, transportation, childcare and utilities, leaving food as the expense they cut back on.

Demand for food banks is rising in other regions of the country, and nonprofits are facing their own operational challenges as they try to meet it.

A spokesperson for the Los Angeles Regional Food Bank told CNBC the organization's diesel bill more than doubled in September, to roughly $75,000, adding to the cost of delivering food and running refrigerated trucks.

Demand in the region is also spiking. Distribution in the Los Angeles area for January through September totaled 116 million pounds of food and grocery products — the equivalent of 93 million meals — and slightly higher than a near-record year in 2025, according to the Los Angeles Regional Food Bank.

Federal food aid changes have exacerbated the problems. Rodriguez of City Harvest described SNAP as a first line of defense against hunger, saying the program can provide as many as nine meals for every one meal the organization provides. But City Harvest has estimated at least 8.7% of SNAP recipients in New York City lost benefits over the past year, after congressional Republicans and President Donald Trump approved work certification requirements and changes to eligibility.

The pressure is also mounting in Los Angeles County, where roughly 260,000 CalFresh recipients are subject to expanded federal work requirements that took effect in June. CalFresh is California's version of SNAP.

That does not mean all 260,000 will lose benefits, since people who meet the work requirements or qualify for an exemption can remain eligible. But a Los Angeles Regional Food Bank spokesperson told CNBC the changes add another layer of uncertainty for households already struggling with food costs.

In Atlanta, the pressure extends beyond the city itself to the surrounding region. The Atlanta Community Food Bank serves about 270,000 households a month, or nearly 700,000 people, through partner pantries across North Georgia. President and CEO Kyle Waide said the number of people it serves has jumped more than 70% in five years.

"Much of that increase is among people whose incomes are too high to qualify for federal benefit programs," said Waide.

Under current SNAP guidelines in Georgia, most households must have gross monthly income at or below 130% of the federal poverty level to qualify. They must also meet a separate net income test. For fiscal 2027, which began Oct. 1, the gross income limit is $2,960 a month for a household of three, or about $35,520 annually, and $3,575 a month for a household of four, or $42,900 a year.

More than 60% of Atlanta Community Food Bank clients have household incomes above the cutoff for SNAP eligibility, Waide said, generally in the mid-to-upper $30,000 range depending on household size. The food bank does not collect everyone's income, he said, but the figure is based on survey estimates.

Given those dynamics, Waide said he does not expect the need to ease.

"We're preparing for the level of demand to stay where it is today, or even increase more," Waide said. "We don't see a big source of relief coming anytime soon."

#308. A First Drive With the Fiat Topolino in New York City

The Fiat Topolino isn't exactly built for New York City. Fiat has been selling this tiny electric vehicle in Europe for three years, but it's now arriving in the US for $14,985 as a street-legal micromobility vehicle. Except it's more like a golf cart than a small EV.

It has a max speed of 25 miles per hour, a 46-mile range, and no airbags. Classified as a “Low Speed Vehicle (LSV),” it can only operate on roads with a posted speed limit of 35 mph or less. (You still need a driver's license, and the Topolino must be registered and have auto insurance.) It also doesn't have a traditional EV charging plug; instead, it uses a 10-foot AC plug that works in any wall outlet—which can be tough if you're in a Brooklyn apartment.

“It's a little bit of an experiment,” says Andrew Waterhouse, head of brand at Fiat USA. “This segment of micromobility—and that's really golf carts—based on the data we have, it's going to grow 28 percent in the next 5 years. People are driving golf carts not to play golf—they're driving them to go to the beach, to go to the clubhouse, to go get coffee, dinner, but they're all just generic. Topolino adds a little bit of that Italian flair and charm, and it's just so unique.”

That’s hard to refute. There's nothing like the Topolino on the market, EV or otherwise. Its adorable looks have drawn the attention of passersby, who've flicked me a thumbs up as I drove past, or pulled out their phones to sneak a quick pic. The Topolino (which is Italian for “little mouse,” and also what Italians call Mickey Mouse) comes with a lot of compromises, but I've had a blast piloting this thing around the city.

From my conversation with Waterhouse, it was clear that Fiat expects to sell more of these Topolino cars in places like suburban Florida. Gated communities, large residences with private land, homes by the beach—you get the idea. There are also hopes to turn the Topolino into a fleet vehicle for campuses and the like. But I wanted to see what it would be like in the bustling streets of New York City. After all, I already drive the Fiat 500 as my personal vehicle.

The Fiat Topolino, left, next to the already small Fiat 500, right.

The first thing that surprised me—other than the minuscule size, which you won't stop thinking about—is how plasticky the thing is. I leaned on it for a second and felt the plastic exterior sink in a little, which immediately made me realize the Topolino won't handle a crash very well; no crumple zones, no airbags—just seatbelts. So yes, don't take this thing on the highway.

It's built for two people and not much else. The passenger can stow a suitcase in front of them, and there's a rack on the back of the car to store another. But besides mesh pouches in the door frames and an elongated glove compartment on top of the dashboard that runs the width of the car, that's about it for storage.

I should also mention the Topolino comes in a few variants: The standard model I tried has full doors and a fixed glass roof, but there's an Open Air model with a roll-back soft-top roof, and the Dolce Vita model has rope doors (aka no doors) and the soft-top roof. You can buy the car in mint, orange, or brownish-gray.

Thankfully, despite my 6'4" frame, I fit quite comfortably in the Topolino. I do have to swing my leg under the steering wheel as I get in, and the seats are a little firm, but the inside feels quite roomy. Only the driver's seat can move forward or back—the passenger seat stays put, and you cannot adjust the steering wheel height.

The asymmetrical, reverse-hinged doors are very unique. The driver's side opens outward from the front, and the passenger door opens the opposite way. There's also a button on each side to open the door, and weirdly, to get out, you pull a fabric strap. Now, the driver-side strap is to the left of the steering wheel, which makes sense, but the passenger-side strap is in an awkward spot behind the seat, near the seatbelt strap. A few of my passengers found that annoying. Also annoying is that you need to use the key to unlock both doors individually—no auto-unlock button plus no key fob. (The car starts with a second key.)

The horizontally split, manually hinged windows flip up, but on rougher roads, they tend to flip back down. You can adjust the small, circular side mirrors and the rear-view mirror, which also doubles as a backup camera display. I have found the backup camera mostly useless, especially at night, when it's just really hard to see what’s going on.

Good thing visibility in the Topolino is excellent, so it's really easy to swing your head around. Unsurprisingly, you can park this thing anywhere. I've parallel parked the Topolino in several tight spots that no other car can fit in, and the lack of parking sensors or the lackluster backup camera didn't bother me. In a city as crowded as New York, that's incredibly valuable.

You should know there's no air-conditioning or heating. There's a windshield fan to defog the windows, which, along with the single wiper and wiper fluid, was useful on cold, rainy days. But in the winter months, you'll have to bundle up, or in the summer, affix a battery-powered (or USB-C) fan to the dashboard. On the dash, you have a simple instrument cluster that shows speed and remaining range, and a built-in phone mount to the right.

You can store luggage on the rack—there's no trunk.

Turn the key to start the car, disengage the parking brake, and tap D or R to start driving. There's no power steering, so turning the wheel requires a little more force than you're used to, and the turn signals don't automatically disengage after you turn. Still, the car feels very responsive. The 8-horsepower electric motor feels fairly quick when you put the pedal to the metal, though you quickly hit the Topolino’s top speed. Good thing the default speed limit in New York City is 25 mph.

But as you start driving, you'll experience arguably the worst thing about the Fiat Topolino: the sound. Because of federal regulations around electric LSVs, the Topolino has a pedestrian alert sound—the kind of angelic hum you might have heard when an electric car is reversing or rolling up to a stop sign. Except the sound is constant, and it gets louder the faster you go. I'm not sure why it's so loud in the car. It feels like it's alerting me more than pedestrians around me.

The sound only disappears if you go past 22 mph, which isn't often, since streets in most cities have a stop sign or traffic light after every block. The first time my wife and I rode in the car, we could barely hear each other talk over the hum. You get used to it over time, but it's very annoying. You can try playing music over it, but the car has no speaker system. Instead, Fiat sells a pair of Monster Bluetooth speakers that you can magnetically stick to the top frame of the car. That works OK, but I didn't like having to keep them charged, so when they died, I played music from my phone. It was sad.

The ride is a little stiff. I drove over one of the worst roads in Brooklyn (Broadway), and you could feel every single bump. When I drove with my brother, they often just exclaimed “Jesus!” every few minutes. Cobblestone was equally pretty bad. But it's doable, and on well-maintained roads, the Topolino was a smooth ride.

New Yorkers rejoice! You legally cannot drive this car into New Jersey. (As if you needed a reason.) All of the bridges and tunnels to the Garden State have speed limits higher than 35 mph. However, I could take the East River bridges to go from Brooklyn to Manhattan, and I did exactly that. Driving over the Manhattan Bridge was a little terrifying when I was holding up a few cars in my lane and everyone decided to race around me. But I got a few thumbs-ups along the way, which helped. Everyone finds this car cute, which goes a long way toward how people treat you on the road.

As for range, it's not great. I wish it were closer to 80 miles instead of 46 miles, especially at this price. It's perfect for quick hour-long round trips around the city; anything longer will give you range anxiety. That trip over the bridge? I went from Bed-Stuy, Brooklyn, to Lower Manhattan and back (around 12 miles). The indicated remaining range went from 46 miles to 30 by the time I got home.

Recharging takes around five hours from zero to full, and the charging cord is built into the car near the passenger-side door. Annoyingly, the 10-foot cable isn't retractable, so you awkwardly have to stuff it back into the door frame when you're done. But the bigger issue is the length. And the standard AC plug. EV charging stations don't typically have AC outlets like the ones in your home. And 10 feet is far too short to reach any apartment or residence in New York City.

Charging the Fiat Topolino requires a standard wall outlet—and, in Brooklyn, probably a long extension cord.

I bought a 50-foot extension cord and ran the cable from my outdoor parking spot to my backyard outlet. It worked perfectly well, but I'm also an outlier, with access to a parking spot and a backyard. Most people don't have those luxuries, so you'll need your own solution.

Initially, after my first ride with the Topolino, I was apprehensive. It felt like I was sitting in a plastic box on wheels, with a blaring sound that wouldn't stop, and every big bump sending a shock into my body. After a week, I was driving the thing everywhere, hand dangling out the half-window, fist-bumping other drivers in bumper-to-bumper traffic, and parking in the tiniest available spots around Brooklyn. Now, a week without the little mouse, I miss it dearly.

It's far from the perfect city car. There are small things I would change to improve the overall rideability. And like the Fiat 500e, it's way too expensive. But as someone who likes their car to stand out, I find so much of what's available in the US market uninspiring. The Topolino breaks the mold. We need more small cars like it.

#305. 8 Best Keyboards (2026): My Honest Picks After Testing Dozens

Keyboards are important. Regardless of how little you might think about yours, you probably use it every day. A keyboard that’s comfortable and easy to use is indispensable and helps you not only do good work—but enjoy doing it as well.

Because we already have a separate guide focused on mechanical keyboards, this list instead places more focus on lower-profile keyboards and other non-mechanical options aimed at a more casual typist. There’s a greater focus on typing comfort and efficiency, instead of typing feel, and less emphasis on customization options like hot-swap sockets or keycap accessibility.

Be sure to check out our other peripheral guides for more, like the Best Mechanical Keyboards, Best Hall Effect Keyboards, Best Mouse, Best Ergonomic Mouse, and Best Computer Monitors.

Updated Noember 2026: I've added the Wallhack K-001 and Keychron K2 HE Concrete Edition to my top recommendations, as well as the Keychron V6 Ultra 8K Hybrid to my honorable mentions. I've also included a couple of recent keyboards I've reviewed that I would suggest avoiding entirely.

One of the highlights of Keychron’s current lineup is its selection of mid-century-inspired keyboards with clean, simple designs and wood highlights. Instead of the standard gamer-y aesthetic, these keyboards offer a more refined style that looks at home on a professional’s desk. The K3 is the first low-profile keyboard in this series, offering a slimmer and more portable typing experience with the same fantastic design language. While this isn’t necessarily the best keyboard on this list by any one metric, I think it’s the most practical option for the largest number of users.

There are two versions of the K3: The typing-focused Ultra and the gaming-focused HE. The Ultra uses standard low-profile mechanical switches, with options for either linear Red switches, or tactile Brown or Banana switches. These switches can be swapped out without any soldering thanks to the hot-swap sockets on the PCB. The switches and stabilizers come lubed from the factory, resulting in typing that feels smooth and offers a consistent, rattle-free sound when typing.

The HE offers only linear Hall effect switches, but these allow for more advanced software customization, such as adjustable actuation distances (how far you press the switch before it registers an input) and Rapid Trigger (which allows for more rapid keypresses by detecting the direction of the switch’s movement). While the enhanced customization of a Hall effect switch is great for gaming, the adjustability won’t be worth the added cost and loss of switch customization for the average user.

The only trade-off with this keyboard is that, compared to a full-size mechanical keyboard, it does lose some travel distance; a low-profile switch is 3.1 mm total, compared with a standard switch’s 4.0 mm. This can be preferable for users who prefer a snappier typing experience or who prioritize a compact form factor.

Both models share the same compact form factor, stylish design, and open-source QMK software for customization, along with the ability to use Keychron’s web-based Launcher for adjusting key mapping and RGB lighting colors.

With Gateron-made KS-TR Hall effect switches and a design that looks straight out of a Dieter Rams–era Braun catalog, I absolutely love this keyboard. The typing experience is fantastic, and this keyboard has a presence on your desk that not many others can match. While the K-001 doesn’t feature a bouncy gasket-mount design, the “stack mount” system it uses (similar to the Wooting 60HE V2 listed below) creates a stiffer, consistent typing feel across the entire keyboard, which I prefer for regular typing.

Beyond that, the K-001 features specs that are competitive with quite a few high-end gaming offerings, with customizable settings for switch actuation distance, rapid trigger functionality, and extensive programmability. It even boasts an 8,000-Hz polling rate and 0.125-millisecond input latency, making it a fantastic choice for even the most competitive gaming. Really, the only thing missing is wireless connectivity, but that’s not a major issue for a gaming-focused keyboard with a hefty CNC aluminum shell.

Another small detail I love is the lighting on this keyboard. Each of the switches is designed to carefully guide the LED underneath to only shine behind the lettering, without any light bleeding between the keys. The LEDs themselves are a well-balanced, neutral white, as opposed to the multicolored RGB found in most keyboards (which often gain a very bluish tint when set to pure white). This all results in a much more minimal and tasteful LED setup compared to the ultra-bright, sometimes overwhelming offerings from other manufacturers.

While the price point is high, especially compared to offerings from more cost-conscious brands like Keychron, this keyboard really is a great object to hold and use, and one that has incredibly robust construction and great engineering underneath the hood.

Keychron’s B2 Pro is one of the best scissor-switch keyboards available, mainly because of the customization it allows. This keyboard uses Keychron’s Launcher, an in-browser software that provides extensive and intuitive customization options for its keyboards, with everything from remapping and macros to multiple function layers. For any type of productivity work, this level of customization can be a great way to optimize an already-good keyboard to one that's perfect for your regular tasks, whether that’s mapping multimedia controls to a function layer or having specific key combinations ready at a moment’s notice.

This keyboard offers a good typing experience for the price, using low-profile scissor switches with a short and snappy key press without being particularly loud or disruptive. The case is made entirely of plastic, and the keycaps are subtly sculpted with a dish (similar to Logitech’s MX Keys line), which makes finding the center of a keycap easier when touch-typing. Because of the low-profile scissor switches, the B2 Pro still feels like a laptop keyboard at the end of the day, which can seem lacking if you’re coming from something with a more robust design.

Slim, durable, and highly customizable, Razer’s Joro is pretty much the most compact gaming keyboard you can find today. It’s thinner than a laptop and just barely thicker than an iPhone, and has the same footprint as a standard 60 percent keyboard, meaning it can slip easily into a backpack, tote bag, or even a large purse. If you were really dedicated, I’m sure it could even fit in the pocket of some cargo pants. The Joro uses Razer’s Synapse software, an incredibly powerful and intuitive customization app that lets you control the keyboard’s RGB lighting, remap any of its keys, and program macros with ease.

The only significant downside of this keyboard is the lack of a 2.4-GHz dongle. This means the keyboard can connect only to devices via Bluetooth or a wired connection. While this isn’t a deal-breaker for me, since the device still has multi-device Bluetooth connectivity, it does slightly hinder the keyboard’s functionality.

In many ways, the Mchose GX87 (8/10, WIRED Recommends) is a “mini” version of the WobKey Crush 80. It has the same layout with similar design choices, and it uses comparable switches and an identical gasket-mount system. However, the GX87 misses out on some of the fancier features of the Crush 80. The colors are e-coated instead of anodized on most models (which creates a less smooth texture), the case is lighter and simpler, and disassembly is generally more complicated.

However, this keyboard still feels great to type on, especially at its budget-minded starting price. If you’re less concerned about some of the style or convenience aspects of a keyboard but still want something that feels great while you're typing, the GX87 is one of the best options available from a per-dollar standpoint. (There are three variants: Lite, Max, and Ultra. Aside from how the colors are coated, the Ultra uses a different switch and has a quick-disassemble design.)

Contrary to what you’d expect from the conceptual absurdity of a concrete keyboard, the Keychron K2 HE (8/10, WIRED Recommends) is genuinely delightful. The design is a bit silly, but that doesn’t get in the way of the performance or the usability of this keyboard. And more importantly, underneath the concrete housing and color-matched keycaps, the internals of this keyboard both feel fantastic to type on (smooth, buttery switches and a solid mounting system make it rigid without feeling harsh) and put down some great specs (2.4-GHz wireless with 8,000-Hz polling and fully customizable Hall effect switches).

But really, what I like best is the material. Using concrete for a keyboard is a bit tongue-in-cheek, and incredibly reminiscent of Soviet-era brutalist architecture—and it won me over. The K2 HE ends up becoming as much of a “Hey, check this out” conversation piece as it is an actual keyboard, and during testing, it put a smile on my face every time I went to use it. That has to count for something doesn't it?

I really don’t understand how Keychron can make a keyboard that has mechanical switches, high-quality keycaps, RGB lighting, and an 8,000-Hz polling rate for under $60. It just doesn’t add up to me. But the company did it, and the resulting keyboard is really fantastic. If you want something with retro styling, comfortable keycaps, and a satisfying typing sound, you really can’t get a better per-dollar value proposition than the C1 Pro. Keychron’s tactile Super Banana switches are poppy and responsive, and the tray-mount case feels sturdy when typing. The only caveat, and this is hardly an issue for most users, is that this keyboard doesn’t have wireless connectivity.

Compared with quite a few other budget-minded keyboards, Keychron’s software is entirely usable and regularly updated. I’ve used quite a few sub-$100 mechanical keyboards with subpar software, with issues ranging from a lack of customization and poor translation to a complete inability to run without hours of troubleshooting. Meanwhile, Keychon Launcher works in-browser, boots up perfectly, allows for extensive customizations, and connects in seconds every time.

The Wooting 60HE is a fantastic keyboard, and the v2 manages to improve on it in almost every way. The polling rate is upped to 8,000 Hz, the switches are updated, and the mounting method has been significantly modernized from the previous tray-mounted design, instead using an isolation mount that both feels better and has a softer typing sound. Plus, the 60HE v2 is one of the few Hall effect keyboards available with a split spacebar, which can be great for both gaming and productivity once you’ve adapted to it.

While it lacks wireless connectivity, basically every other aspect of this keyboard is as good as it gets: The 60 percent layout uses standard designs that are common in the aftermarket, allowing for easy upgrades to the case, and the v2 is one of the few mainstream Hall effect keyboards to use a standardized type of switch, meaning it can be easily swapped out with countless aftermarket options. In-software customization of actuation distance, multi-input, and quite a few other cutting-edge settings means you won’t be wanting for gaming performance, either. The only thing to watch out for is the compact 60 percent layout, which saves a lot of space but won’t be for everyone.

Keychron V6 Ultra 8K Hybrid for $164: By introducing a true “hybrid” keyboard, Keychron has resolved its largest issue with Hall effect keyboards: lack of customization. Along with being compatible with standard MX-style mechanical switches, Keychron also claims the V6 is compatible with “95 percent of mechanical switches on the market.” Although it’s hard to prove that number exactly, this opens up a vast world of customization possibilities, along with providing significantly more options for repairs in the event of a switch failing. Beyond this, it also means you can have access to both mechanical switches with a tactile bump and highly customizable Hall-effect switches without needing two keyboards.

Happy Hacking Keyboard Classic Type-S for $222: The Happy Hacking Keyboard lineup has never been known for cost-effectiveness. This is shown especially with the Pro Classic Type-S, a nearly-$300 keyboard with wired-only connectivity and a distinct lack of bells and whistles. However, the unique layout and Topre switches can pretty much only be found here, and make for a unique tactile typing experience that can’t be matched by many other keyboards. Plus, the massive aftermarket community for Topre keyboards means both repair and customization are incredibly easy and well-documented. They’re a bit pricey, but one of these keyboards could last the rest of your life with a bit of care.

Wooting 80HE for $200: While the technology falls a bit behind the 60HE V2, the 80HE’s larger layout still makes it a fantastic option for anyone who isn’t quite ready to get rid of their F-row and arrow keys. The switches feel great, the magnesium case is incredibly robust, and the Wootility customization interface is both straightforward and incredibly powerful.

Logitech Pro X TKL for $140: Logitech makes great keyboards, and the G Pro X TKL is among the best gaming keyboards. It has vibrant RGB LED-backlit keys, a choice of clicky, tactile, or linear switches, and it uses Logitech’s Lightspeed wireless adapter for competitive gaming-level response time. The build quality of this keyboard is slick and stylish. It’s minimal and doesn't take up much space on your desk, and it has a subtle metallic rim around the edge that gives it a little flair that most plain keyboards lack. The volume wheel in the upper right is smooth and easy to reach, and along the top are handy media controls so you can pause your music when you finally get into a game after a long queue. For my tastes, the more clicky-clacky a keyboard, the better, and the Black Clicky switches have served me well. Each keypress feels like I'm sending tiny thunder down to my game. However, if you prefer something softer, you can choose another switch type. The only thing I dislike is the lack of a numpad—yes, I’m one of those weirdos who prefer having a numpad.

Logitech Pro X 60 for $130: The Pro X 60 (8/10, WIRED Recommends) has virtually all the benefits of the Pro X TKL in a smaller, more compact package. It keeps the volume wheel, Game mode switch, and Bluetooth/Lightspeed buttons by moving them to the edges of the keyboard, while slimming the whole thing down to a 60 percent layout.

Logitech Pop Keys for $67: The Pop Keys (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is a vibrant line of wireless keyboards that come in a wide variety of color palettes that are delightful. It also uses Logitech's system for pairing with up to three devices, making it simple to take it between your PC and laptop, or from home to work and back.

Logitech MX Keys S for $110: The MX Keys S can pair with three devices, making it easy to swap between computers. Its low-profile chiclet-style keys are comfortable, and it uses proximity sensors to activate the key backlight when your hands get near, so it's easier to see in the dark without wasting battery when you’re not using it. It supports both Mac and Windows layouts, and the keys are tastefully labeled in a way that it’s clear no matter which one you’re using at the time. Battery life is also fantastic, lasting well over a week with normal use, though it gets quite a bit longer life if you disable the backlight.

Logitech MX Mechanical for $142: With an understated, low-profile design, you can pair the MX Mechanical with up to three devices at once and swap with the push of a button. There are even a few convenient extra buttons just above the numpad to launch a calculator or lock your desktop.

Turtle Beach Vulcan II TKL Pro for $150: The Vulcan II TKL Pro has two LEDs per key, giving it a better resolution for lighting effects. It features Hall effect switches, which should cut down on wear and tear. They’re still satisfyingly clicky, and the volume knob has a comfortably grippy texture. I prefer any keyboard with a volume wheel to one without.

Corsair K65 Plus for $100: This 75 percent keyboard has some of the softest, most comfortable keys of any board I’ve tested. It’s lightweight enough to toss in a bag but sturdy enough to be your desktop keyboard. It can connect via USB-C, Bluetooth, or a wireless dongle that can be stored in a slot on the rear. A stylish metal volume knob adorns the top-right corner, and every keycap and switch can be swapped out using the included removal tool.

Razer Huntsman Mini for $65: A 60 percent keyboard has 60 percent of the keys normally found on a regular-size keyboard. The numpad and arrow keys are chopped off, and you’re left with the essentials. The Razer Huntsman Mini is one of my favorites of this size for gaming. It feels every bit as responsive and quick as a full-size keyboard, but it takes up a lot less desk space. There’s just something neat and orderly about it. Plus, like the larger Huntsman Elite, the Mini is compatible with Razer’s keycap kits, so you can customize your color scheme.

Keychron Q1 HE for $212: The Keychron Q1 HE (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is one of the best boards we’ve tested that uses Hall effect switches. You can customize the actuation point to either make keys more sensitive—so you don’t have to press them all the way down for keystrokes to register—or less sensitive, to avoid those fat-finger moments that can ruin competitive games. Keychron even has rapid-trigger settings that allow you to press a key multiple times without the key having to return fully to its resting position. Even outside the benefits of the Hall effect switches, this is another great keyboard in line with the kind that Keychron is known for, so it’s worth a look even if you don’t want to pay that much attention to every aspect of your keys.

NZXT Function 2 for $50: The original NZXT Function was a great way for anyone interested in mechanical keyboards to jump in without getting overwhelmed. The follow-up Function 2 (8/10, WIRED Recommends) improves on it in almost every way. It upgrades the keys to optical switches and comes with a spare set of switches that have a little more (or a little less) resistance, so you can customize specific keys based on your needs. I found this particularly useful for games like Overwatch 2, where I’d like to cut down on those fat-finger ultimates that are so embarrassing. The Function 2 retains many of my favorite features from the first model. It has the same left-side volume roller, super-soft keycaps, and convenient buttons along the side of the keyboard. If you’re interested in mechanical keyboards but are intimidated by phrases like “actuation force,” this is a great board to get started with.

Razer Huntsman V3 Pro TKL for $132: The Huntsman V3 Pro TKL is a robust keyboard for those who like to tweak their gaming setup. It uses Razer’s analog optical switches, which are satisfyingly clicky. On the top right, there’s a media knob that controls the volume, which you can also click to mute. However, it’s the buttons around it that are most interesting. To the left, there are two programmable macro keys you can use to customize different commands for your games (or your work). Below, on the navigation keys, are six profile shortcuts. Hold Fn and press one of them, and you can swap between several preset profiles, tailored to specific gaming needs like FPS mode, Racing mode, or High-Sensitivity mode when you need to pull off that hair trigger. All of this can be customized in the Razer Synapse app. We’ve tested a lot of keyboards with different customization options, but this one is particularly good for gamers who swap profiles a lot. The keyboard connects using a USB-C cable, included with the device, and it also comes with a magnetic wrist rest.

Razer BlackWidow V4 75% for $126: The Razer BlackWidow V4 (8/10, WIRED Recommends) has a sturdy metal casing, hot-swappable switches, and Razer’s robust Synapse software for customizing your keyboard. It’s also earned our top marks if you’re looking for a mechanical keyboard specifically for gaming. The 75 percent layout is small enough that you can leave plenty of room for your mouse, making those flicks to land a headshot that much easier in competitive games. The 8,000-Hz polling rate also helps cut down on the times that you miss activating an ability by that almost imperceptible fraction of a second.

SteelSeries Apex Pro for $150: Rather than choose one switch for the Apex Pro keyboard, SteelSeries decided to allow them all. Not only is it a colorful gaming keyboard with lots of bells and whistles, but it also features mechanical switches that can be customized per key to give you a typing experience unique to you. Plus, it has a little LED display for system alerts, volume, and other fun stuff you can toy with using SteelSeries’ included software.

Keychron Q16 Ceramic Keyboard: Unlike the other novelty-focused keyboard on this list, the Keychron Q16 (5/10) falls a bit short in terms of user experience. The outer case and the keycaps are made of a plasticky ceramic that feels unpleasant to type on, and the sound profile is equally underwhelming. Ultimately, this keyboard feels less like an earnest effort and more like an attempt to chase the trend of ceramic keycaps from brands like Cerakey.

Logitech G512 X 98: While a hybrid mechanical/Hall effect keyboard may sound like a great all-around solution, it really only works as a regular keyboard when the feeling between the switches stays consistent. That’s exactly where this keyboard falls short: The “tactile” model I tested only had mechanical switches with a tactile bump, while the Hall effect switches were linear. When trying to type or do other productivity work, the two ended up constantly clashing. This means you either have to put up with an unpleasant typing experience or you’ll always have to swap out switches and recalibrate when moving between work and play.

Razer Pro Type Ergo: While this keyboard is solid and feels good to type on, the $200 price point seems far too high for what it is. Having a plastic case and laptop-like chiclet-style 66 keys, it won’t blow your socks off. Unless you desperately need Chroma RGB lighting, or have some other reason to stay within the Razer ecosystem, there are much more affordable options that offer nearly identical usability.

Generally, keyboards are defined by two specific design choices: the layout and the type of switches they use. A switch is the mechanism underneath a key that controls how the switch is pressed down. The layout can easily be seen by looking at a keyboard, but the switches can be a bit more difficult to guess from general observation. Here are the most common you’ll see:

Scissor switches are among the most widespread types of keyboard switches available today, found in nearly every consumer laptop and countless slim keyboards, including the Apple Magic Keyboard. These switches are incredibly compact and have a short travel distance, which makes them ideal for anything portable. Their low profile, flat shape, and short travel distance means they can be quick to type on, but they often lack the enjoyable tactile experience of a thicker keyboard. These switches are often also referred to as chiclet switches, a not-quite-accurate name that comes from the small amount of space between each key.

Membrane switches are one of the least expensive switches to manufacture, and are widespread even today in schools and offices. They typically consist of a sheet of rubber domes with electrical contacts inside of them, which then have keycaps put on top. When one of these keys is pressed down, it compresses the rubber dome and registers a key press. These keyboards are waterproof and reliable, but they have a key press that is typically described as mushy and unpleasant.

Mechanical switches are fairly widespread in enthusiast circles, but the actual definition of a “mechanical” switch is debatable. However, for this guide’s purpose, a “mechanical switch” will typically refer to a switch that uses the same design as a Cherry MX switch and has a metal “leaf” on the inside, which is two pieces of metal that are pressed together to register an input. ThereminGoat has a great in-depth guide on how a mechanical switch works and what all the components do. There are three main types of MX-style mechanical switches, tactile, linear, and clicky, that we discuss in-depth in our mechanical keyboard buying guide.

Low-profile mechanical switches rely on principles similar to a standard mechanical switch, but they compress the movement into a much shorter switch. They typically have a shorter key press, use unique keycaps, and are less standardized than full-size mechanical switches. Because they’re shorter, they are typically used for either low-profile keyboards or uniquely shaped keys on a standard keyboard (like the mouse buttons on the HHKB Studio).

Hall effect switches are typically similar to mechanical switches in shape, and will feel comparable to type on, but the key difference is how they register an input. A mechanical switch requires physical contact between two components, while a Hall effect switch uses magnets and sensors to determine whether a key has been pressed down. With most Hall effect keyboards, the sensor can detect how far the key has been pressed, and you can actually program the keys to only register an input at a certain distance, or even to register multiple inputs at different distances. By comparison, a standard mechanical switch will only register an input at a predetermined distance. While a Hall effect switch may seem like an all-around upgrade compared to a mechanical switch, there is still a trade-off: Nearly every Hall effect switch available is linear, which means there is no bump or click when the keyboard registers an input. Beyond that, because of small differences in their internal designs, many enthusiasts prefer the typing feel of a mechanical switch.

There are so many factors to consider when picking the right keyboard for your needs that it can get overwhelming. Not everyone has the same needs, and many aspects of a keyboard can seem universally desirable to some while being utterly polarizing to others. Here are a few things to keep in mind:

Mechanical, or no? If you like big, clicky keyboards with raised keys that make a statement, mechanical keyboards might be for you. This is also a rabbit hole that many nerds have lost themselves in, so it can be overwhelming to dive into the nuance of all the different styles in this subgroup. If you’re more a fan of the flat, chiclet-style keyboards found on low-profile keyboards (and laptops), you can save yourself a lot of time by skipping the mechanical keyboard rush. On the other hand, if you do want mechanical, we have a few in this guide you can check out, but we also have a dedicated Best Mechanical Keyboard guide you should peruse.

Wireless or wired? Wired keyboards have the advantage of never dying and never needing to be charged up. The disadvantages are, well, obvious. If you need a wireless keyboard to take with you to the office and back home, or just want more flexibility on your desk, then make sure to check a keyboard's battery life, what kind of batteries it uses (rechargeable is usually better), and what kind of system it uses for recharging.

Wireless connectivity options. Some wireless keyboards use a 2.4-GHz USB dongle to connect to your PC or laptop, which often means more reliable signal strength, while others use Bluetooth to connect to a wider range of devices. Bluetooth keyboards in general are pretty great these days, so it’s not a huge sacrifice, but pay attention to how you need to connect the keyboard to your devices when making a purchase.

Number of device connections. Similarly, some wireless keyboards can remember multiple devices they connect to and swap between them with the press of a button. If you have a desktop, a laptop, and a work computer you want to use one keyboard with, it’s a good idea to check how many devices your keyboard can remember when making your choice.

Polling rate. As mentioned, this refers to how often per second your computer receives a signal from your keyboard. Modern keyboards already approach 1,000 Hz (or once every millisecond), which is faster than what most people ever need. However, if you play a lot of fast-paced competitive games online, having a higher polling rate (commonly approaching 8,000 Hz, or eight checks every millisecond) can reduce the time between when you press a key and when the game registers it. Which, when you're dodging headshots, can mean the difference between life and virtual death.

Software. With most keyboards today advertising extensive customization options, it’s important to be sure these adjustments can be done easily and quickly. Some keyboards have great customization software with explanations, tool tips, and intuitive systems to make adjustments, and some don’t. Software like Razer Synapse, Keychron’s Launcher, and Wooting’s Wootility are some of my favorites, and I’d definitely recommend doing some research on your keyboard’s software before locking in your choice.

Hz, or hertz, refers to the polling rate of a keyboard. In essence, this number is how many times the keyboard communicates with your computer in one second. Your average computer peripheral operates at 125 Hz, while higher-end equipment with a focus on speed can operate upwards of 1,000 Hz. Realistically, for everyday use, 125 Hz is perfectly serviceable. Having something higher can be beneficial for gaming, and can potentially feel smoother, but the difference is not as important as you would think.

2.4 GHz, short for 2.4 gigahertz, is a radio frequency that computer peripherals use to communicate wirelessly with a USB dongle. Most keyboards with 2.4-GHz connectivity will also have Bluetooth connectivity, but there are many keyboards that have Bluetooth without 2.4 GHz. There are many differences between how the two operate and how they perform, but the main ones are connection quality and convenience. A Bluetooth connection will often operate at a lower polling rate, such as 125 Hz or 250 Hz, but can connect directly to a Bluetooth-enabled device without a dongle. A 2.4-GHz connection, on the other hand, can operate at much higher polling rates (some devices exceed 1,000 Hz) but will require a USB port to plug a dongle into. For either connection method, the wireless range is dependent on the individual device.

Gasket mounting is a method of keyboard construction that has become popular in recent years. In a gasket-mounted keyboard, the internal assembly of the keyboard is not directly screwed into the case. Instead, rubber gaskets are placed along the edges of the top and bottom halves of the case. These press together around the internal assembly and hold it in place once the two halves have been screwed together. This allows the internal assembly to move up and down slightly when typing, along with absorbing the vibrations of typing. This kind of assembly typically results in a softer and more satisfying typing experience, while also improving the sound of the keyboard by removing any extra noises.

Function layers are secondary layouts on a keyboard that allow for inputs that don’t have dedicated keys on the keyboard. These are often accessed by holding down a key labeled “Fn” or “Function,” then pressing another key. Function layers allow for multimedia controls, setting adjustments, or access to keys like F1 through F12, or arrow keys, if they were removed from the keyboard to save space.

I test each keyboard on this list for an extended period of time: at least a week, and often longer. I test each under a diverse set of conditions including gaming, writing, internet browsing, video and photo editing, and even some programming. During this, I take extensive notes on how a keyboard behaves, what works, and where I run into trouble. Once I’ve finished testing a keyboard in real-life situations, I compare it to other keyboards to see how it stacks up, and I typically try to disassemble each keyboard and critique its internal assembly.

When determining what goes in this guide, I take multiple different aspects into account. The largest priorities to me are build quality, typing experience, and ease-of-use: A solid keyboard that feels good to type on will typically score better than a flimsy and boring keyboard, even if the flimsy keyboard has fantastic software, style, or typing sound. However, all of these metrics come into consideration, and if a keyboard totally fails in a certain category, that can still take it out of the running.

Keyboards are subjective, so I try to approach each review with an open mind. Even if I don’t like typing on a keyboard, I always try to imagine a user who might like it, and I evaluate its design choices from that perspective along with my own. Ultimately, you will know better than anyone else whether a keyboard is a good fit for you.

#304. Best Buy reports comparable sales growth of 6.1%, highest in five years

Best Buy on Tuesday beat Wall Street expectations on the top and bottom lines for its third fiscal quarter and raised its full-year guidance.

The consumer electronics retailer reported comparable sales growth of 6.1%, a significant beat over expectations of 2.3%, according to market intelligence platform StreetAccount. The company said that growth was its highest in five years. It reported a domestic comparable sales increase of 6.2% and international comparable sales growth of 4.9%.

"We have a tremendous amount of momentum," CEO Jason Bonfig told CNBC. "The fact that we saw pretty much broad-based growth across almost all of our categories is a lot of momentum that we're very excited about."

Best Buy also raised its guidance for the rest of the year. It's now expecting full-year revenue of between $43 billion and $43.3 billion compared with a previous expectation of between $42.3 billion and $42.8 billion. It's expecting comparable sales to be up 3.4% to 4% compared with prior guidance of between 1.9% and 3%.

The earnings report is the company's first since Bonfig took over as CEO from Corie Barry at the beginning of the month.

Bonfig said the retailer saw overperformance in both computing and gaming for the quarter, driven by recent game launches and a targeted product assortment.

Looking ahead into the holiday season, he said the Best Buy consumer remains "resilient," but that they are focused on getting value wherever they can.

"We did see not only our current customers continue to be engaged, but we actually did see more new customers come into the brand, as well as we had some customers that we re-engaged as well," Bonfig said. "So those are really, really positive signs for us in Q3, and all of that was factored into the way that we guided for Q4 and the rest of the year."

Here's how the company performed in the period ended Oct. 31 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Best Buy reported net income of $353 million, or $1.66 per share, compared with $140 million, or 66 cents per share, the year prior. Adjusting for one-time items, including restructuring charges, Best Buy posted adjusted earnings of $1.62 per share.

#301. Here’s Everything You Can Do With With the New Gemini AI on Android Auto

Google Assistant is being replaced by Google’s more advanced Gemini AI across all platforms, and that includes Android Auto. If the switch hasn’t happened yet on your own vehicle’s dashboard, then it should happen soon.

You’ll see a message onscreen announcing the arrival of Gemini, with the new “spark” icon (a small star by a sound-wave-like icon), instead of the traditional microphone when the AI is active.

If you've used Gemini before on your phone, on the web, or somewhere else, then you're going to know the extras that it brings over Google Assistant. It's a truly natural conversation partner that can dig deep into information available online, and respond to a much wider range of queries. Here's what the upgraded app can do specifically when you're traveling on the road.

All of the standard commands you might have already been using are still here, of course, like "navigate home" or “Where's the nearest Walmart?” With Gemini though, there's much more flexibility in what you can say without the AI getting confused or misunderstanding what you're asking about.

For example, your questions can be multilayered. Something like "find the nearest coffee shop that has a drive-thru and is open now" will look for those exact criteria. You're also able to ask context-sensitive follow-up questions, such as "What time will it shut?" or "How long will it take to get there?" if you need further details.

You can ask more general questions too, such as "tell me more about the place I'm heading to" or "Is there outdoor seating?” But bear in mind that Gemini will be limited to scouring the data on Google Maps for its information. (It's a disembodied AI that's never been anywhere.) If it doesn't know the answer to something, it should tell you that.

Overall, it's smarter in every aspect. I was recently navigating a difficult junction and couldn't work out whether the map was sending me left or right. I asked Gemini, "Will I be traveling east or west after the next turn?" and it figured out the answer. That helped me avoid veering off in the wrong direction.

One of the major benefits of having a voice-controlled AI in the car is having it handle messaging and audio tasks without you needing to take your eyes off the road or fish around for a button. If you tell Gemini to “read my last message,” it'll speak it out for you and give you the opportunity to reply. You can also specify the app, otherwise Google Messages will be used by default—Google Chat and WhatsApp are among the others that are supported.

Gemini is able to give you summaries of group chats, which is really handy when you're on a drive and the conversations you're involved in are building up message after message that you can't check. Name a group chat in a supported app and ask for a summary, or just request summaries of unread messages. You'll be able to get the gist without checking each individual message.

The usual array of audio commands are here, carried over from Google Assistant, so you can quickly start or stop audio in your music, podcast, radio, and audiobook apps. As well as continuing from where you left off, you can also name artists, albums, and playlists that you want to queue up. YouTube Music and Spotify are among the apps supported, if you need to specify one.

Another extra from Gemini is being able to ask about the artist or song that's currently playing, and get more information on it. You might want to learn the history of a particular band, find out how long a certain song was at number one, or even get recommendations based on what's currently playing—just ask Gemini.

Much more than Google Assistant, Gemini can help you learn something or develop some ideas while you're behind the wheel. If you're on the way to a movie premiere, you can ask Gemini about the history of the film, the director, and the actors, and it'll remember the context of your conversation. (It'll all get synced back to the Gemini app on your other devices.)

Voice commands such as “help me prepare for my interview” or “come up with ideas for a quick and easy meal to make for dinner" will initiate a chat with Gemini that you can continue throughout your journey—and hopefully arrive well-prepared or with dinner sorted (or whatever it is). Maybe don’t ask about anything too mind-bending, as you’ll still need to concentrate on driving.

Gemini will ask along the way for any information it needs about what you’re interviewing for or the ingredients you’ve got at home. You can also ask Gemini to quiz you on a certain topic or run a query on something you see on the journey—like a landmark or a restaurant you go past.

Finally, there’s always the weather: Gemini will give you forecasts for the areas and specific locations you give it, on whatever day you want within the next week or so. Perhaps more useful for journeys are questions like “When is the rain going to stop?” or “What are the weather conditions like at my destination?” which will help you plan your trip.

#299. Retail turnarounds are taking hold just in time for the holiday season

Once-struggling retailers are entering the holiday quarter with improved performance and sales momentum as turnaround efforts begin to resonate with shoppers.

A handful of earnings reports on Tuesday pointed to a mix of factors behind the strong results, including a resilient consumer, stronger execution and demand for the right products at the right price.

Kohl's reported comparable sales growth of 1.2% for the period ended Oct. 31 and raised its full-year outlook as CEO Michael Bender said customers "have remained resilient" but are "migrating to value with their purchases."

He tied improvement to the company's work on product assortment, store experience and value.

Best Buy also on Tuesday posted its highest comparable sales growth in five years, at 6.1%, which prompted the electronics retailer to raise its full-year outlook.

"We have a tremendous amount of momentum," CEO Jason Bonfig told CNBC in an interview. "The fact that we saw pretty much broad-based growth across almost all of our categories is a lot of momentum that we're very excited about."

The company also credited execution, market share gains and a compelling product cycle alongside growing customer demand.

At Dick's Sporting Goods, quarterly comparable sales rose 2.6% at the core business and 0.5% at Foot Locker. CEO Lauren Hobart said "all income demographics grew" and the company "didn't see trade-down from best to better or better to good."

She similarly pointed to new products and market share gains within the category as contributing to the strong quarter. She also highlighted continued improvement at Foot Locker.

All three companies have been undergoing efforts to boost sales and get the right products on shelves to meet customer demand.

Target, likewise undergoing revitalization efforts, last week reported comparable sales growth of 5.6% in the third quarter, fueled by a 5% increase in comparable traffic. The retailer raised its full-year outlook.

CEO Michael Fiddelke at the time called the traffic gain "a healthy sign that guests are responding to our changes and choosing Target more often."

Even Gap CEO Richard Dickson told CNBC the company has moved from "rebuild mode" to "turnaround mode" at its Old Navy banner, a sign of progress, albeit not a broad-based portfolio recovery.

Michael Baker, a retail analyst at D.A. Davidson, told CNBC he sees both a resilient consumer and company-specific improvements as driving sector strength.

"Retail sales have been more resilient than most think," Baker said. His analysis showed retail sales, excluding autos and gas, rose 5.1% in the third quarter on a nonseasonally adjusted basis — the strongest quarter since the pandemic.

But he cautioned that growth appears to be coming more from transaction size than traffic, with inflation, promotions and higher units per transaction driving up spend.

Dollar Tree, which reported better-than-expected earnings on Tuesday morning, posted a 3.8% increase to traffic, accelerating from 0.4% growth in the prior quarter, suggesting more shoppers may be bargain hunting. Comparable sales at the retailer increased 4.6% during the period.

"Consumers are under pressure, and they are increasingly selective about where and how they spend," said Dollar Tree CEO Michael Creedon on the company's earnings call. "When under pressure, shoppers prioritize value and buy closer to need."

Comparable sales of everyday essentials rose 8.9% at Dollar Tree stores in the third quarter, while sales of nonessential items were essentially flat, the company said.

— CNBC's Laya Neelakandan contributed to this report.

#297. The Best MagSafe Wallets for Your Everyday Carry (2026)

The best MagSafe wallets are compact, slim, and svelte, and they attach securely to your iPhone (or MagSafe-compatible case). They are handy if you only want to carry a few cards, like your work badge or train fare. MagSafe wallets are also great for anyone who wants to travel light and forgo a traditional wallet entirely. We’ve tested dozens, and our favorites are below.

Read our MagSafe guides for more useful accessory recommendations, including the Best MagSafe Accessories, Best MagSafe Power Banks, Best MagSafe Wireless Chargers, and Best MagSafe Grips.

Updated November 2026: I’ve added new wallets to our honorable mentions section and removed discontinued products. I’ve also checked for accuracy throughout.

MagSafe is Apple’s magnetic technology built into the iPhone 12, iPhone 13, iPhone 14, iPhone 15, iPhone 16 (excluding the iPhone 16e), iPhone 17, iPhone 18 Pro, and iPhone Duo. It features a hidden ring of magnets on the back of the phone and was developed to create a faster, more precise wireless charging system. Those magnets also connect to accessories such as external batteries, car mounts, and wallets.

If you use a case on your iPhone, make sure it’s also MagSafe (the case will have a ring of magnets inside). This will ensure a proper connection with MagSafe accessories. If you use a non-MagSafe case, the connection will be very weak, and MagSafe products may just slide off your iPhone. We have lots of case recommendations in our guides:

When buying a wallet, make sure it supports MagSafe or Qi2 connections. The product description should indicate this prominently. Qi2 is the wireless charging standard, and all MagSafe iPhones support Qi2. Android phones now also support Qi2, and some have magnets inside, like the Google Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 series (Google calls it Pixelsnap).

MagSafe wallets use the same ring of magnets that lets them snap directly onto the back of the iPhone or a MagSafe- or supported Qi2 case. This gives the wallet a strong and secure hold on your device. The wallets we’ve included in this guide all have the MagSafe seal of approval.

Apple first introduced MagSafe for its iPhones in 2020. The following models support the technology:

Do MagSafe Wallets Work With Android Phones?

To use a MagSafe wallet with an Android phone (or the iPhone 16e), you’ll need to use a MagSafe case. Several case manufacturers have started adding a ring of magnets to Android phone cases to bring the same magnetic experience native to iPhones.

Will a MagSafe Wallet Demagnetize My Credit Card?

No, MagSafe will not demagnetize your credit cards. Credit cards have magnetic stripe encoding strong enough to resist demagnetization, and the MagSafe wallets in this guide include a built-in shield designed to keep your cards safe. However, you may run into issues with hotel key cards and some gift cards. Keep those away as a precaution.

I use a MagSafe wallet every day as my primary wallet. I check that it snaps firmly onto the iPhone or MagSafe case—and that it doesn’t slide off when I take my phone out of my pocket, bag, or jacket. I also make sure cards fit well in the sleeve and don’t fall out. I only recommend wallets that feel durable, are easy to use, and can hold the standard amount of cards (at least two to three). I occasionally call on my fellow WIRED reviewers for long-term testing or to check out new models.

UAG’s Metropolis MagSafe wallet is on the spendier side, but you won’t be replacing it in a year or two. It is lightweight yet robust with Kevlar construction. There’s a large slot on the back that can hold up to three cards, and you can unfold the wallet and store an additional three (or cash) inside. It also pulls double duty as a stand if you need to prop up your phone, and you can orient your phone in landscape or portrait mode. —Molly Higgins

Smartish’s MagSafe wallet makes me wish all wallets had a slot on the side to push out the cards. I never had to take it off my phone to access cards. Just give the spacious side opening a little push with your thumb, and the cards slide out. My cards remained secure, and I never had an issue with them falling out. It’s made of vegan leather, and Smartish offers a few fun designs. —Brenda Stolyar

This luxe, super-thin leather MagSafe wallet from Nomad has Apple’s Find My feature built in, so you can easily locate it in the Find My app if it’s misplaced. That does mean you need to charge the wallet, but don’t worry, there's no proprietary cable here. Instead, the wallet can be wirelessly charged on any MagSafe or Qi2 charger; once it’s fully charged, the battery lasts for five months. Easy peasy.

It’s made from vegetable-tanned Horween leather with a polycarbonate frame, and it can hold up to four cards. (A less expensive version that uses Nomad's Camino leather is also available.) It looks classy, and it’s great for anyone with a tendency to lose things. —Molly Higgins

Note that Nomad also sells a dedicated tracker card, which can add Find My to any wallet but will take up valuable space in a MagSafe version.

I love this wallet from Moft, which is compatible with Apple Find My, so you always know where it is. It’s relatively standard-looking, but it has a built-in tripod, which came in handy numerous times when I wanted to film a quick outfit check or take a group photo. It raises your phone camera to 8 inches high, and the wallet is very sturdy, so you can dial in the right angle. It works in landscape or portrait orientation. With space for two cards, it isn’t the roomiest but is rich in features. —Louryn Strampe

You can always rely on Casetify for unique designs. Its Snappy MagSafe wallet is available in various styles and colors. It’s slim, durable, and sleek—the illustrations haven’t faded after months of use. It’s made from vegan leather (aka plastic), but Casetify uses BioVeg, derived from recycled polyester and vegetable oil from non-food and GMO-free corn crops.

It can hold up to three cards, and there’s a built-in shield that protects them from magnetic damage. My only gripe is that it can be a little difficult to pull the cards out when the wallet is attached to your phone or case. I typically have to detach it and use the opening from the back to slide out the cards. —Brenda Stolyar

Ridge’s metal MagSafe wallet feels solid and high-quality. A few of us tested it, and it reliably held our setups, including one tester’s daily carry of eight cards plus a thicker tracking card. The magnets could be stronger, but Ridge does sell a strengthening tray that might be useful if you’re concerned.

This wallet can be a little weird to use at first, but you build up muscle memory quickly. There’s a finger slot for pushing cards out, and you slide them back in on the opposite side. Ridge also includes a Torx screwdriver and extra screws, which are useful for switching out the plates, adding or subtracting room for cards, or adding on accessories like the brand’s wallet chain or cash strap. —Louryn Strampe

Most MagSafe wallets are designed to hold just a few cards, but I love the Moft Snap Field because it can hold so much more. You get plenty of storage space for cards—technically up to eight cards, though more reasonably seven—alongside a dedicated slot for an extra SIM card and a SIM card ejector.

That extra room already puts the Snap Field a step ahead of most other MagSafe wallets, but you can also store just about anything you want inside. It uses a folding design held together by magnets, so you can quickly throw in cash, coins, or paper cards. Regardless of what you store inside, you can easily get to your cards with a pull tab. And, if all of that wasn’t enough, the backing that attaches to your phone can pop out and function as a kickstand. —Jacob Roach

ESR’s MagSafe wallet isn’t bulky, but it also isn’t so thin that it feels insubstantial. It doubles as a kickstand and sticks to my phone reliably. There’s space for five cards—three in the external pockets, plus another two on the inside. I really like the clear window that keeps my ID separate and handy to flash when I get carded. This wallet is simple, but that’s the beauty of it, and it’s affordable to boot. If you want something basic, it’s a good option to consider. Just keep in mind that the included RFID-blocking card probably isn’t necessary. —Louryn Strampe

Casely’s wallet is made of hard silicone, so it’s slightly heavier and thicker than the other ones I’ve tested. It feels similar to having a MagSafe battery pack on the back. I don’t mind the extra weight and thickness because it makes it easier to grip my phone case. There’s a dedicated slot at the bottom that makes sliding cards out a breeze. Just know that if you pair it with the complementary Casely case, the whole thing is bulky. But darn if it doesn’t look cute. —Brenda Stolyar

I’m obsessed with PopSockets grips—I have one on my phone and one on my Kindle. If you’re also a fan and don’t want to get rid of the accessory with a MagSafe wallet, well, you don’t have to. The Popwallet+ is both a PopSockets grip and a wallet. It fits up to three cards (or more, depending on the thickness), and the cloth opening at the bottom makes it easy to push out the cards. The grip works the same way a standard one does, with the ability to expand and collapse. You can swap out the tops if you ever get bored with the design. —Brenda Stolyar

Supcase’s MagFlip wallet and stand is extremely sturdy, and feels unbreakable. It’s constructed almost entirely out of metal, fitted with huge magnets that never let go and thick hinges around the body. You can store up to five cards in the wallet itself, and there’s an RFID-blocking card that sits at the end, though this kind of protection is largely unnecessary.

It doubles as a two-height stand as well. You can kick the wallet back and prop your phone up, but if you rotate the wallet around, you can position your phone even higher with a kickstand that keeps everything stable. Even with the rugged, almost militarized construction, SupCase still offers a handful of attractive colors, including one that combines a faux leather exterior with regal gold accents. —Jacob Roach

A lot of MagSafe wallets just feel like a pocket on the back of your phone. This one from ESR feels like an actual wallet. It comes in a variety of stylish options with a slick metal-tipped clasp and detailed construction. There’s a clear window for your ID, a roomy card pocket, and a compartment that can hold two bills. The card compartment can technically hold up to four cards, but I prefer two or three for easier access. If you want space for cash as well as the other essentials, or you want a leather-type wallet that has more design choices than some competitors, I recommend this one. —Louryn Strampe

Looks like you need some MagSafe for your MagSafe. Look no further than the Valentinus wallet from Spigen. It’s constructed out of polyurethane leather and can technically hold three cards (I’m able to easily fit four). It comes with a handy card cutout at the bottom so you can quickly thumb through them. The real draw is an extra MagSafe ring built into the back of the wallet.

Stack a MagSafe grip on the back, mount your phone to a MagSafe car stand, or attach whatever other MagSafe accessory you want; you don’t need to take off your wallet first. You can’t charge your phone through it, but the convenience of using other accessories while keeping your wallet attached is worth the price of admission. —Jacob Roach

Moft’s Snap-on Phone Stand and Wallet is another good kickstand wallet option. You can set it up at three angles: one for scrolling through your phone, one for streaming media, and one for video conferencing. It feels sturdy, and the case isn’t bulky. I wouldn’t put more than two cards in this one, though. I usually use it to carry my license and debit card, while the rest are in my Apple Wallet. —Brenda Stolyar

Alternatively, Moft sells a trackable version with Apple Find My capabilities. It even comes in versions that can match your iPhone. It isn’t super roomy, but I still like it.

ESR Geo Wallet Stand for $47: Apple’s Find My app lets you track your devices if they’re lost, and ESR’s Geo wallet has it built right into the wallet itself. This is the wallet I’ve been using for the past few weeks, and outside of its Find My capabilities, I love that it strikes a great balance between size and usability. ESR says it can hold up to three cards, but I’ve been using mine with four—three cards plus my ID—and I can get them all out easily. Although having a wallet with magnetic charging pins is weird—the Find My feature requires a battery that lasts three months—you can turn it off if you don’t care for it (but then, maybe just buy a different wallet). It does kind of suck that you need a proprietary charger to recharge your wallet, though. The magnets adhere well to the back of the phone, and you can pop open the wallet and use it as a kickstand. ESR even includes a strap on the back that works as a phone grip.

OtterBox Symmetry Series Cactus Leather MagSafe Wallet for $45: This wallet is nice and simple, thin, lightweight, has a strong hold on my phone case, and offers a dedicated fabric-covered slot at the bottom to push the cards out (I was able to fit three without much trouble). This OtterBox wallet is made from cactus-based leather, which feels nearly as luxurious as real leather. Just know that cactus leather isn’t as eco-friendly as it’s made out to be—these cases are still infused with layers of plastic.

Spigen MagSafe Classic LS Wallet for $40: This cool-looking wallet incorporates design inspiration from the classic Macintosh computers. The gray might seem a little bit drab, but any Apple enthusiast will likely enjoy the nod to the computers of yesteryear. It’s otherwise pretty standard fare, with space for up to three cards. I like the thumb notch, which makes it easy to slide your cards out.

Pelican Protector MagSafe Wallet: This MagSafe wallet is simply too bulky. It’s difficult to slip into a pocket, and we don’t think the protective hardshell is worth the trade-off since it can only hold two or three cards.

Kate Spade New York Morgan MagSafe Wallet: This wallet looks nice, but the finish starts to degrade with regular use. It also opened on its own once or twice, which left me worried about a card slipping out.

Ohsnap! Snap Grip Wallet: I had high hopes for this one, mainly because of its build quality. The wallet is aluminum, can hold up to eight cards (depending on whether they have raised lettering or not), has MagSafe support, and comes with a grip that doubles as a kickstand. Unfortunately, the grip is made of plastic, and it broke after a short time (it won’t fold properly back into place). The magnetic hold isn’t as strong as other MagSafe wallets, even with a MagSafe-approved case on my phone. None of that is great, especially at this high price.

Apple FineWoven MagSafe Case: Any time this wallet is separated from your iPhone, you’ll get an alert and can track it in Apple’s Find My app. It has a single slot that fits up to three cards, but to remove them, you have to take it off your iPhone and push the cards up through the slot on the back. Unfortunately, Apple’s MagSafe wallets use only the company’s proprietary FineWoven material (made from recycled materials). It’s a commendable effort to reduce reliance on leather production, but several WIRED reviewers have said the material doesn’t hold up well over time.

Journey Loc8 Universal MagSafe Slim Wallet: My cards would slip out of this wallet if I didn’t have it stuffed full, which makes it an obvious “Do Not Recommend” choice when so many other comparable wallets don’t have this problem.
